'''Fritz Joseph Ursell''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Abrahams | first1 = I. D. | last2 = Martin | first2 = P. A. | title = Fritz Joseph Ursell. 28 April 1923 -- 11 May 2012 | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2013.0005  | doi-access = free| journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]]| volume = 59 | pages = 407–421 | year = 2013 | s2cid = 72445938 }}</ref> (28 April 1923 – 11 May 2012) was a British [[mathematician]] noted for his contributions to [[fluid mechanics]], especially in the area of wave-structure interactions.<ref>{{harvtxt|Ursell|1994}}</ref> He held the [[Beyer Chair of Applied Mathematics]] at the [[Victoria University of Manchester|University of Manchester]] from 1961 to 1990,<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Abrahams | first1 = I. D. | last2 = Martin | first2 = P. A. | last3 = Norris | first3 = A. N. | title = G.R. Wickham: An appreciation | doi = 10.1016/S0165-2125(00)00059-7 | journal = Wave Motion | volume = 33 | pages = 1–6 | year = 2001 | issue = 1 | bibcode = 2001WaMot..33....1A }} This contains also information on Fritz Ursell and the Beyer Chair.</ref> was elected [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1972 and retired in 1990.<ref name="mathgene">{{MathGenealogy|id=133292}}</ref>

==Education==
Ursell came to England as a Jewish<ref>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Ursell|title=Fritz Joseph Ursell
}}</ref> refugee in 1937 from Germany,<ref name="Ursell_975"/><ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Cambridge University Press| isbn = 978-0-521-41414-2| last1 = Martin| first1 = P.A.| first2 = G.R. | last2 = Wickham| title = Wave Asymptotics: The Proceedings of the Meeting to Mark the Retirement of Professor Fritz Ursell from the Beyer Chair of Applied Mathematics in the University of Manchester| year = 1992| page = xi}}</ref> and was educated at [[Marlborough College]].<ref>{{Who's Who | title = URSELL, Prof. Fritz Joseph | id = U38391 | type = was | volume = 2025 | edition = online}}</ref> From 1941 to 1943 he studied at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], graduating with a [[bachelor degree]] in mathematics.

==Career==
At the end of 1943 Ursell joined the [[British Admiralty|Admiralty]] as a part of a team—headed by [[George Deacon]] —whose task was to formulate rules for forecasting waves for the allied landings in Japan. Their findings have become the basis of modern [[wave-forecasting]]. Ursell stayed in the Admiralty until 1947. In 1947 he was appointed to a [[post-doctoral]] fellowship in applied mathematics
at Manchester University without a [[doctorate]]. In 1950 he returned to Cambridge as [[lecturer]]. There he met [[G. I. Taylor]]. In 1957 he spent a year at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], having been invited by [[Arthur Ippen]]. In 1961 Ursell moved back to Manchester.<ref>{{Cite book | publisher = World Scientific | isbn = 978-981-02-1950-5 | last = Ursell | first = Fritz | title = Ship Hydrodynamics, Water Waves, and Asymptotics: Collected Papers of F. Ursell, 1946–1992 | year = 1994 | series = Advanced Series on Fluid Mechanics }} In two volumes, 1004 pp.</ref>

In 1994 Ursell was awarded the [[IMA Gold Medal|Gold Medal]] of the [[Institute of Mathematics and its Applications]] in recognition of his "outstanding contributions to mathematics and its applications over a period of years".<ref>{{cite web|title=IMA Gold Medal|url=https://ima.org.uk/awards-medals/ima-gold-medal/|access-date=16 May 2018}} Institute of Mathematics and its Applications</ref>

== Scientific work ==
In 1957 he published together with Clive R. Chester and Bernard Friedman a classic paper that introduced a method to find [[asymptotic expansion]]s for contour integrals with coalescing saddle points.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Clive R.|last1=Chester|first2=Bernard|last2=Friedman|first3=Fritz|last3=Ursell|publisher=Cambridge University Press |title=An extension of the method of steepest descents |journal=Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society |volume=53 |number=3 |date=1957 |pages=599–611 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100032655|bibcode=1957PCPS...53..599C |s2cid=122589439 }}</ref> The method is now called [[method of Chester–Friedman–Ursell]].

==Personal life==
Fritz Ursell was married to Katharina Renate Zander in 1959. They had two daughters.<ref name="Ursell_975"/> Susie and Ruth, Susie is married and has two children.<ref name="Times_obituary"/> Following his death on 11 May, in hospital, Ursell's funeral took place on 15 May 2012 at Manchester Crematorium.<ref name=Mactutor>{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Ursell/|title=Fritz Joseph Ursell|publisher=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]]|author=J J O'Connor and E F Robertson|date=March 2014|access-date=4 June 2021}}</ref>
